1: Every choice in a plan should be justified by its effect on the uncertainty, not just its name. A good plan explains how each variable is controlled and how the data will be used.
2: Systematic errors shift every reading in the same direction, while random errors scatter them. Recognising which is present tells you whether repeats will help or a different method is needed.
3: A graph that is a straight line gives the physical quantity from its gradient or intercept. Plotting the right pair of variables linearises a relationship, so the gradient can be measured reliably.
